title: RLVR landscapes for iterated multiplications can be benign: Insights from spin-glass theory

paper.title: RLVR landscapes for iterated multiplications can be benign: Insights from spin-glass theory
paper.abstract: Abstract Despite the importance of reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR), the extent to which it can learn new reasoning capabilities remains debated. Here we study the optimization landscape of RLVR on algorithmic tasks, such as iterated group and quasigroup multiplication. To this end, we map entropy-regularized RLVR over myopic tabular policies onto an energy-based (spin-glass) model over deterministic policies. This mapping upper-bounds what RLVR can achieve, and lets us rigorously characterize the landscape in this tabular setting. We show, both theoretically and experimentally, that for a wide class of models and tasks with uncorrelated inputs, this landscape is benign, containing no local minima that could trap RLVR training. Rather, the practical difficulty of these tasks appears to stem, at least in part, from issues such as diffusive barriers and gradient-estimation error in traversing the landscape. These are genuine obstacles that can prevent a solution from being found, but they are distinct from the landscape itself being rugged. We show that these obstacles can often be mitigated through the choice of entropy regulator. Consistent with this theory, we find that a transformer trained from scratch, using only last-token rewards, successfully learns an algorithmic chain of thought for iterated non-Abelian group multiplications.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR), policy-gradient training against an automatically checkable success signal, is the main tool behind recent improvements in the reasoning of large language models ( DeepSeek-AI, 2025 ; Yu and others, 2025 ) . Whether it produces genuinely new reasoning, or mainly reweights behavior already present in the pretrained model, is debated ( Yue and others, 2025 ; Wu et al., 2026 ; Wen et al., 2026 ; Tsilivis et al., 2025 ) . Behind this debate sit open optimisation questions about RLVR itself. Due to the credit assignment problem, intermediate tokens receive little to no direct signal, and sampled gradients are noisy ( Yu and others, 2025 ; Tao et al., 2025 ; Han and Yang, 2026 ; Li et al., 2026 ) . Such hurdles can be, in principle, addressed by larger batches, dynamic sampling, and difficulty curricula ( Yu and others, 2025 ; Jiang et al., 2025 ) , but these are not generic cures. Curricula, for instance, are subject to primacy bias and shortcut learning ( Nikishin et al., 2022 ; Liu et al., 2023 ) . Indeed, practitioners routinely describe runs as “trapped in a local optimum” ( Wang and others, 2025b ; Jin et al., 2026 ) . This brings to question the complexity and ruggedness of RLVR landscapes. Such analyses of reinforcement learning exist for specialized settings (see related literature), which show that optimizing policies with bounded memory is NP-hard in the worst case ( Littman, 1994 ; Mundhenk et al., 2000 ; Vlassis et al., 2012 ) . However, worst-case statements say little about typical instances. For random constraint satisfaction problems, analysis of the typical case was pushed forward by applying statistical mechanics approaches based on spin-glass theory. For instance, spin-glass theory traced typical-case algorithmic hardness to the geometry of the solution landscape, which above certain thresholds breaks into many separated clusters and local minima ( Mézard et al., 2002 ; Krzakala et al., 2007 ; Zdeborová and Krzakala, 2016 ) , inspiring rigorous mathematical approaches ( Gamarnik, 2021 ) . Building a similar bridge between spin-glass theory and RLVR is thus a desirable goal. As a toy setting to approach this goal, we focus on a simple class of algorithmic tasks consisting of iterated quasigroup and group multiplication ( Liu et al., 2023 ; Merrill et al., 2024 ; Li et al., 2024 ; Grazzi et al., 2025 ; Marchetti et al., 2026 ) . This choice is partially motivated by a simplistic reading of what pretraining provides: a set of skills ( Michaud et al., 2024 ) the model can execute individually, together with the problem of composing them in the right order. Taking the skills to be the elements of a finite group or quasigroup and composition to be its operation, “learning to reason” becomes evaluating a product of T T elements presented in sequence, with one intermediate token emitted per element and reward only if the final token is the correct product. As model classes, we use myopic tabular policies (myopic in the sense of DeWeese and Qu (2026) ) that read a bounded window of the input together with their own recent tokens. While such myopic bias is obviously a crude approximation to that of a transformer, the workhorse of RLVR applications in reasoning, it has several merits: It fleshes out culprits in the RLVR loss itself rather than in the policy parametrization. It exhibits some of the qualitative features seen in transformer traps for our tasks, while permitting essentially exact numerics. In this work, we provide a novel spin-glass perspective on RLVR, which allows an in-depth analysis of the above task with some conclusions carrying over to transformers. In particular, we establish the following results A mapping between RLVR and spin models (Sec. 3 ). We build a dictionary between RLVR and spin-glass models, yielding three results: every local maximum of the reward is continuously connected, without crossing a loss barrier, to a deterministic policy, referred to as a code or spin-configuration (§ 3.1 ); with an entropy regulator, the RLVR loss is provably lower-bounded by the free energy of a corresponding spin-glass energy-based model (§ 3.2 ); and steady states of local dynamics on the spin-glass model’s trapped configurations approximately coincide with RLVR fixed points (§ 3.3 ). Spin-glass model for parity task is solvable (Sec. 4.2 ). We obtain closed expressions for the free energy of the spin-glass model associated with parity at any temperature and depth ( T T ) and find a first-order phase transition at large T T , between strictly random and correct codes. Reward landscapes can be benign (Sec. 4.1 ). We leverage the spin-glass mapping to prove that for simple untied models the reward has no suboptimal local maxima. We show that a simple Monte Carlo sampler of the spin-glass models solves all untied models and tasks without a curriculum. With weight tying and input correlations, the proof breaks down, and indeed we find local maxima. The RLVR–spin-glass gap and regulator choices (Sec. 5 ). We show that RLVR optimization (via exact local policy updates) fails to optimize untied models, while as aforementioned, Monte-Carlo on spin-glass models succeeds. This gap is due to the former’s inability to diffuse over equal reward code landscapes. We show that this gap can be closed with local policy resets to random deterministic policies or strong regulators. Strongly regulated transformers solve the task (Sec. 5.1 ). We show numerically that transformers can easily express and interpolate between untied tabular policies with narrow windows and hence share some of their benign landscape features. We further show transformer trained from scratch on the same task fail when left weakly or moderately regulated, but often yield perfect learning of the task when strongly regulated and augmented by a curriculum to circumvent signal-to-noise issues.

sections.heading: Additional related literature.
sections.text: Landscape analyses of reinforcement learning exist for specialized settings: gradient-domination results for complete parameterisations ( Agarwal et al., 2021 ; Bhandari and Russo, 2019 ) , the linear-quadratic regulator ( Fazel et al., 2018 ) , convergence for softmax tabular policies ( Mei et al., 2020 ) , and a study of what entropy regularisation does to small exact-gradient problems ( Ahmed et al., 2019 ) . Our work is close in spirit but distinct from the maximum-entropy formulation of control, in which an entropy-regularised objective is read as inference over a Boltzmann measure on trajectories ( Ziebart et al., 2008 ; Levine, 2018 ; Haarnoja et al., 2018 ) : there the sites are the time steps of a rollout, whereas our ensemble is over policies and the sites are table cells. On the physics side, a glassy phase was demonstrated for an optimal-control landscape ( Day et al., 2019 ) , spin-glass language has been applied by analogy to supervised loss surfaces ( Choromanska et al., 2015 ) , and reinforcement learning has been used as a solver for spin-glass ground states ( Fan and others, 2023 ) . The trapped configurations we certify have antecedents as partial pooling equilibria in signalling games ( Lewis, 1969 ; Crawford and Sobel, 1982 ; Huttegger et al., 2010 ; Skyrms, 2010 ) , as miscoordination of independent learners in common-payoff games ( Panait and Luke, 2005 ; Matignon et al., 2012 ) , and as myopic optima of restricted policy classes ( DeWeese and Qu, 2026 ) . Entropy collapse in RLVR and entropy-management schemes are active empirical topics ( Cui and others, 2025 ; Wang and others, 2025a ; Yang et al., 2026 ) ; the diagnostics here differ in being derived from measured landscape structure rather than fitted to online statistics. The stalls of plain RLVR and their repair by re-randomisation are the multi-step counterparts of partial pooling and its destabilisation by mutation ( Zhang, 2004 ) and are kept from premature fixation by margins acting as mutation.

sections.heading: 2 Setting: Task and Models
sections.text: Let 𝒜 \mathcal{A} be a finite alphabet of size q q carrying a binary operation B : 𝒜 × 𝒜 → 𝒜 B:\mathcal{A}\times\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{A} whose multiplication table is a Latin square, i.e. every row and every column is a permutation of 𝒜 \mathcal{A} . Such a structure is a quasigroup ; a group is the special case in which B B is also associative. The input is a sequence x 1 ​ … ​ x T x_{1}\ldots x_{T} drawn uniformly from 𝒜 T \mathcal{A}^{T} (in some expereimental setups we break this assumption and draw correlated inputs), and the target is the left fold s 1 = x 1 , s t = B ⁡ [ s t − 1 , x t ] , target = s T . s_{1}=x_{1},\qquad s_{t}=B[s_{t-1},x_{t}],\qquad\text{target}=s_{T}. (1) We refer to s t s_{t} as the state of the task at step t t . To solve this task, we consider models that sequentially generate an output sequence y = ( y 1 , … , y T ) y=(y_{1},\ldots,y_{T}) conditioned on the input x x . At each token index t t , the next token y t y_{t} is drawn from a distribution, or policy, π \pi that can depend on x , y < t , t x,y_{<t},t . An optimal policy is one that perfectly outputs the target, y T = s T y_{T}=s_{T} , regardless of intermediate tokens. In this section, we define two model classes for this task: tabular policies trained with RLVR (Section 2.1 ), and an energy-based model for the distribution of deterministic policies (Section 2.2 ).

sections.heading: 3 Mapping the spin-glass model to RLVR
sections.text: Up to this point, we have made no explicit connection between the RLVR objective and our energy-based spin model. In this section we make this comparison more rigorous. We show that the local maxima of the reward as a function of policies are continuously connected to codes with the same reward; we then use the spin model to obtain a bound on the RLVR loss, which is important for regulator effects at finite temperatures; and we show that the Monte Carlo sampler’s traps in the spin model coincide with local minima of RLVR training.

sections.heading: 3.1 Spin-Glass Codes as Reward Maximizers
sections.text: Our first result is given by the following statement Statement 3.1 . We consider the space of policies as a product of simplices embedded in ℝ q × | 𝒞 | \mathbb{R}^{q\times|\mathcal{C}|} . Let π ∗ \pi^{*} be an untied policy such that there exists an open set around it where π ∗ \pi^{*} obtains a maximal reward, then it can be connected by a continuous path of fixed reward to a deterministic policy σ ∗ \sigma^{*} such that J ⁡ ( σ ∗ ) = J ⁡ ( π ∗ ) J(\sigma^{*})=J(\pi^{*}) . We show this for a simplified case here; the full proof follows a similar structure (App. B ). Let π ∗ \pi^{*} locally maximize J J , and let c c be a cell that the code consults with at which π c ∗ \pi^{*}_{c} is non-deterministic. For simplicity, suppose only two actions a , b a,b are possible at this cell, with π c ∗ ​ ( a ) = s \pi_{c}^{*}(a)=s , π c ∗ ​ ( b ) = 1 − s \pi_{c}^{*}(b)=1-s . By multilinearity of J J , we have, up to constants, J ∝ s ​ Q ​ ( c , a ) + ( 1 − s ) ​ Q ​ ( c , b ) J\propto s\,Q(c,a)+(1-s)\,Q(c,b) . Since π ∗ \pi^{*} is a local maximum of the reward, we require Q ⁡ ( c , a ) = Q ⁡ ( c , b ) Q(c,a)=Q(c,b) , so J J is constant in s s , and we are free to assign any probability we wish to a a and b b . The edge cases s ∈ { 0 , 1 } s\in\{0,1\} are codes. The proof in App. B extends this approach to policies with larger support and more cells.

This ansatz is typically correct when each spin interacts with many other spins, as is the case for our model. sections.heading: 3.3 Spin-Glass Pure States as Training Traps
sections.text: In spin-glass theory, it is well established that Monte Carlo sampling tends to become trapped in pure states : configurations in which σ c \sigma_{c} and σ c ′ \sigma_{c^{\prime}} are approximately uncorrelated for c ≠ c ′ c\neq c^{\prime} ( Mézard and Montanari, 2009 ) . The full distribution over spins can then be understood as a mixture over such pure states. Since these pure states are, by definition, fully factorized across cells, they lie within the same variational family π ^ = ⨂ c π ^ c \hat{\pi}=\bigotimes_{c}\hat{\pi}_{c} considered above. Among all such factorized distributions, the most likely pure states are precisely those that locally minimize the variational free energy F var F_{\text{var}} . Thus, we expect that when Monte Carlo converges to a steady state, the corresponding distribution would have weakly correlated spins, and its marginals per cell would be approximate solutions to Eq. 4 . In Fig. 2 we demonstrate empirically that this is indeed the case for the trapped models that we studied. sections.heading: 4.1 Untied classes hold no defended minima
sections.text: A key empirical result of this paper is that, for a wide class of untied models, namely untied ( 0 , 0 ) , ( 2 , 1 ) , ( 1 , 1 ) , ( 3 , 0 ) (0,0),(2,1),(1,1),(3,0) window models with uncorrelated inputs, the landscape has no local minima, as evidenced by Monte Carlo optimization at vanishing temperature consistently sampling codes with J = 1 J=1 . See Tab. 2 for full results. Here we support this with the following analytical result Theorem 4.1 (local search reaches optimal reward) . Consider the untied ( 0 , 0 ) (0,0) window (i.e. c t = ( x t , y t − 1 ) c_{t}=(x_{t},y_{t-1}) ) class on a quasigroup fold with inputs drawn uniformly, and local dynamics that change one cell at a time and accept any change that does not lower J J . From every code there is a finite chain of accepted changes ending at a code with J = 1 J=1 . The proof (Appendix E ) proceeds in two parts. First, we show that a collision-free code, one in which no two histories in different task states are ever assigned the same output token, reaches J = 1 J=1 in a finite number of steps that do not decrease the reward. Second, we show how to remove collisions iteratively, without ever decreasing the reward. At a colliding step, every cell is first set to the token that is individually optimal for the true state it leads to. Since there are exactly q q possible true states and q q possible tokens at this step, any two states left sharing a token after this adjustment leave exactly one token unused. We show how the code can be set to route through the unused token without decreasing the reward. Applying this at each successive colliding step, and then treating the resulting collision-free code by the first part, proves the theorem. Corollary 4.2 A non-decreasing reward escape path exists also in policy space when starting from a code. Proof: Note that due to multilinearity of J J , a linear extrapolation between π c \pi_{c} and π c ′ \pi_{c}^{\prime} , with rewards J J and J ′ J^{\prime} respectively, results in a linear interpolation of the reward. Since the theorem relies only on such local policy changes, it implies a piecewise linear extrapolation in policy and reward space. Corollary 4.3 A non-decreasing reward escape path exists from any policy. Proof: If the policy is in a local maximum, it is connected to a code via statement 3.1 . If it is not in a maximum, then, by definition, a path with improving rewards exists.

sections.heading: 4.2 Exact solution for parity
sections.text: Section 3.2 showed that the spin model’s free energy bounds the RLVR loss, without evaluating that free energy explicitly. sections.heading: 5 Further Experimental Results
sections.text: The results of previous sections raise several natural questions that are addressable numerically. The first concerns the tightness of our bound and the importance of diffusive-barrier or barren plateaux in the landscape. In Table 2 we measure that difference at negligible temperatures, showing that for many untied tasks RLVR falls much below the spin model which consistently obtaines near perfect reward. The success of the Monte-Carlo sampling suggests that diffusive barriers for the spin model are mild. This apparent gap motivates us to look for potential improvements on the RLVR side (see App. G.5 for further detail). The success of Monte Carlo samplers motivates the use of periodic resets as a direct means of expediting diffusion. The existence of a phase transition in the parity task motivates us to consider large regulator coefficients (temperatures) to reduce free-energy and entropic barriers. Figure 3 , left panel, shows the results of these, with about half the models responding well to high entropy regulator levels. Resets (solid markers) work even better for this class. The inset table summarises reset interventions of the same class ( 2 % 2\% of the cells redrawn uniformly every 10 10 iterations for 100 100 cycles): the reward attained and the τ \tau of the run it summarises. (b) The one-block transformer under the gated curriculum, REINFORCE with an entropy bonus β \beta (occupancy convention), read as greedy accuracy on held-out inputs of length 8 8 at the final step. One point is shown per seed, bar is the mean over seeds. The transformer has no direct counterpart of tabular cell resets. From a different angle, the lack of a reward barrier in the landscape motivates us to look for variations of the task that induce such barriers. We consider tied tables or correlated inputs, wherein the inputs are drawn from a Markov chain with a k > 1 / q k>1/q chance of emitting the previous token. Both variations violate different lemmas of our escape proof, and indeed in Tab. 6 , we numerically establish the existence of true energy barriers. We note in passing that, for tied models, these barriers are microscopic yet common. Namely, they have a reward barrier equal to failing on a few specific input combinations, but occur for most initialization seeds. For correlated inputs, barriers are macroscopic but rare (i.e. involve a finite fraction of input combinations but only occur for about 12 % 12\% of initialization seeds).

sections.heading: 5.1 Transformers on the same task
sections.text: We consider tabular policies as a toy model for transformers, which raises a natural question: do the escape paths we establish for tabular policies also exist for transformers trained with RLVR? We would expect an affirmative answer if two things hold: a transformer can express a tabular policy, and it can traverse the escape route between one code and the next without losing reward. We show below that both do hold. Motivated by these results, we train transformers on the same tasks under sufficient entropy regularization, and show that they often converge to J = 1 J=1 consistent with a benign landscape (Fig. 3 panel b). Starting with expressivity, we verify that a modest 791 791 k-parameter transformer can be brought to express random untied tabular policies, with wider windows taking longer to train, suggesting an implicit bias favoring narrow tables (see App. G.4 , Table 3 ). We further test how well such a transformer follows an escape path of Monte-Carlo. To this end, we locate distinct codes in the chain, train a transformer on one such code ( σ i \sigma_{i} ), save its weights ( θ i \theta_{i} ), then fine-tune it on the next distinct code ( σ i + 1 ≠ σ i \sigma_{i+1}\neq\sigma_{i} , on visited cells) and obtain the resulting weights ( θ i + 1 \theta_{i+1} ). Notably, such fine-tuning never fails to reach perfect agreement: At T = 6 T=6 , all 189 189 points reproduce their code exactly on all 5 6 = 15,625 5^{6}=15{,}625 inputs. We then consider a linear interpolation between θ i \theta_{i} and θ i + 1 \theta_{i+1} and test whether this incurs a drop in reward along the path. Interestingly, for the large majority of sequential codes — 159 159 of 180 180 steps — no such drop is observed, and for the remaining small fraction the drop in the reward is at most 2 × 10 − 3 2\times 10^{-3} . See Tab. 4 and App. G.4 for further details. The above results suggest transformers should inherit the simplifying landscape features of untied tabular models. Motivated by this, we study the effects of strong entropy regulators (standard occupancy-weighted regulator) on the same three tasks as in the tabular setting, together with curriculum learning to prevent signal-to-noise issues. As discussed in App. G.5 and shown in Fig. 3 , without a regulator, and at every coefficient up to β − 1 = 0.1 \beta^{-1}=0.1 , no seed of any task holds more than length T = 2 T=2 and every seed is at chance at length T = 8 T=8 . At β − 1 = 0.3 \beta^{-1}=0.3 five of eight seeds on ℤ 5 \mathbb{Z}_{5} and three of eight on the quasigroup pass 0.95 0.95 at length T = 8 T=8 , and they carry the curriculum far beyond it, to T = 18 T=18 on ℤ 5 \mathbb{Z}_{5} and to length T = 20 T=20 on three of the quasigroup seeds. Notably, regulator choices here far exceed standard practice ( Ahmed et al., 2019 ; Cui and others, 2025 ) , by one to two orders of magnitude. Around β − 1 = 0.3 \beta^{-1}=0.3 , the policy carries 42 % 42\,\% of the maximum entropy ( ln ⁡ 5 \ln 5 ). We note in passing that before this strong regulator choice, we made many changes to optimization (REINFORCE,GRPO,Expert-Iteration), curricula, adaptive batching, eps-exploration, and combinations thereof, all failed to learn at T = 4 T=4 .

sections.heading: 6 Discussion
sections.text: In this work, we established a mapping between RLVR on tabular models and a spin-glass model whose spins take values in action space and sit at cells/table-entries. Configurations of spins amount to deterministic RL policies. The spin-models appear to enjoy a larger degree of tractability compared to the original RLVR problem, and their free energy lower-bounds the RLVR loss. Gaps between plain RLVR and these lower-bounds motivated us to consider strong regulator effects. Surprisingly, they facilitate RLVR training from scratch for both tabular models and transformers. We further describe several scenarios in which both the spin-model and RLVR end up trapped in valleys of the loss. We hope to leverage this framework to further study fundamental limitations of RLVR. In particular, it would be interesting to apply it to harder algorithmic tasks which may require invoking the full spin-glass framework, replica-symmetry breaking included. In addition, it would be interesting to incorporate the effects of pre-training and implicit biases of more complex architectures via the inclusion of prior terms. Limitations. Pure tabular models are a rough caricature of transformers and thus offer only a qualitative link. We further focused on untrained models, based on the concept of skill compositions. Extending this to real pre-trained models carries in much complexity. While prior terms, including K ​ L KL -penalties, can close some of these gaps qualitatively, their specific relation to RLVR training of networks remains to be studied. The strong regulator choices which facilitated learning here are likely damaging for actual pre-trained models. While some elements of spin-glass theory have been used here, in particular the notion of pure-states and their link to local Monte-Carlo updates, it is yet to be determined whether important concepts such as replica symmetry breaking carry through to these specialized spin models.

sections.heading: Appendix C The code spin model and its relation to the RLVR objective
sections.text: This appendix separates the correspondence used in Section 3 into its three components: (i) a spin model defined on deterministic policies, with no reference to stochastic policies; (ii) the Gibbs–Bogoliubov variational bound for that model over product trial measures, which produces an objective of reinforcement-learning form; and (iii) an identity showing that this variational objective coincides with the true RLVR objective of the stochastic policy, under a single-visit condition that we state and verify. Components (i) and (ii) are standard statistical mechanics ( Mézard and Montanari, 2009 ) ; component (iii) is elementary but, to our knowledge, not available in the literature in this form, so it is derived here in full.

sections.text: The spin-glass has an exact symmetry, which is easiest to see in matrix form. The matrix formulation fleshes out several structures distinguishing our model from standard spin-glass models — by which we mean a system such as the p p -spin model, whose multi-variable couplings are drawn at random between sites, and sites are placed on a complete or random hypergraph. In contrast to standard spin-glass systems, this grid has no notion of locality. Another source of difference from standard spin-glasses is that the factors coupling the Σ \Sigma ’s can become effectively lower order when a finite set of Σ \Sigma ’s becomes rank-1. For instance, if Σ t 1 , x t 1 \Sigma_{t_{1},x_{t_{1}}} becomes rank-1 for all q q values of x t 1 x_{t_{1}} (e.g. Σ t 1 , x t 1 = [ 1 , 0 ​ … ​ 0 ] ⊤ ​ [ 1 , 1 ​ … ​ 1 ] \Sigma_{t_{1},x_{t_{1}}}=[1,0\ldots 0]^{\top}[1,1\ldots 1] ), then the factor becomes q − T ∑ x u s T ​ ( x ) ⊤ Σ T , x T ⋯ Σ t 1 + 1 , x t 1 + 1 [ 1 , 0 … 0 ] ⊤ q^{-T}\sum_{x}u^{\top}_{s_{T}(x)}\Sigma_{T,x_{T}}\cdots\Sigma_{t_{1}+1,x_{t_{1}+1}}[1,0\ldots 0]^{\top} . sections.heading: E.3 Remarks, verification, and scope
sections.text: A strictly defended code admits no improving move among consulted cells; its first escape is Step 2’s preparation move at an unconsulted cell, which gradient-based dynamics can never make, since by Statement 1 the gradient at a cell with w c = 0 w_{c}=0 is identically zero. The argument extends verbatim to any product measure with full support, including position-dependent marginals, a claim we have verified numerically (12 of 12 random codes driven to the weighted optimum under random Dirichlet marginals). We expect the same argument to extend to wider untied windows, with the window’s information state in place of the message, though this is left for future work. At present, the wide-window case is supported only by the measurements of Section 4.1 . The two assumptions that cannot be removed, bijectivity and independence of the inputs, are the subject of the next two subsections.

sections.heading: E.4 What breaks under weight tying and correlated inputs
sections.text: Tie the tables across steps, one shared entry σ ( x , m ) \sigma_{(x,m)} consulted at every step, and the proof fails at two named places, in increasing order of severity. (i) Statement 1 fails: under tying, the entry being moved can itself be consulted again at another step for a different input, so the continuation value no longer separates cleanly from the entry being changed. The single-visit condition of App. C restores the affinity of J J in each entry but not this separation across inputs. (ii) Step 2 fails, in two ways. First, a token unused at step t t may still be in use at another step, since it is the same shared entry; the pigeonhole argument therefore no longer guarantees a free token, as the unused slot is occupied by an entry another step depends on, and zero-cost preparation is gone. Second, even where an unused token is found, rerouting one state onto it revalues every other state that shares that same entry at a different step, so the switch is no longer guaranteed to leave other cells unaffected, and the term-by-term improvement argument fails. In summary, the untied chain cannot hold a defended suboptimal policy because every entry serves exactly one role, so idle capacity carries no cost to reassign, preparation carries no cost to perform, and repairs affect no cell beyond the one being repaired; weight sharing removes all three properties at once. The structural fact underlying Statement 1, that which cell an input consults depends only on its history, with every continuation equally likely, fails: the continuation law now depends on the history through the current symbol. Consequently, cells sharing an outgoing state no longer share continuation values, since the value becomes joint in state and symbol, and consolidation cannot be repaired even by collective moves: the incumbent routing realises the average of per-symbol maxima, while any common token realises at most the maximum of the average.

sections.heading: Conventions used throughout.
sections.text: Where a policy is stochastic, the reward J ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] J\in[0,1] is computed from its committed (greedy/argmax) action at every cell unless the text says otherwise. Rewards are always averaged over all input combinations and contain no estimation errors. Certified traps are codes/spin-configurations in which no single-cell change raises the reward, and no path of reward-neutral single-cell changes reaches a code from which one does. For our simple models, we test for these with exact search algorithms. Parity refers to the Z 2 Z_{2} group, quasigroup refers to the following 5-element Latin square B = ( 1 3 4 0 2 3 1 0 2 4 4 2 3 1 0 2 0 1 4 3 0 4 2 3 1 ) , s t = B ⁡ [ s t − 1 , x t ] , B\;=\;\begin{pmatrix}1&3&4&0&2\\ 3&1&0&2&4\\ 4&2&3&1&0\\ 2&0&1&4&3\\ 0&4&2&3&1\end{pmatrix},\qquad s_{t}=B[s_{t-1},x_{t}], (41) whose five column permutations generate S 5 S_{5} . The Metropolis kernel draws a proposed action for the visited cell uniformly over all q q actions — including the one the cell currently holds, so a cell may stay put — and accepts it with probability min ⁡ { 1 , e Δ ​ J / τ } \min\{1,e^{\Delta J/\tau}\} , where Δ ​ J \Delta J is the exact change in expected reward. sections.heading: G.2 Stationary distributions of MC are approximately CAVI fixed points
sections.text: In the main text we argue that, given that all spins interact with all spins, local (single-spin) Monte-Carlo updates from a single random initialization should end up in a stationary distribution (a pure state) in which spins are approximately uncorrelated. This appendix tests this heuristic on two models and at different temperatures. Specifically, we focus on traps with J < 0.99 J<0.99 . sections.heading: G.3 The RLVR Monte-Carlo gap
sections.text: Strictly speaking, the spin model acts as a lower bound on the attainable RLVR loss (Eq. ( 8 )). While in the experiments of App. G.2 the stationary distributions of Monte Carlo were close to RLVR fixed points, the reverse statement typically fails to hold: RLVR at vanishing temperature often stops at a lower reward than Monte Carlo on the same class. sections.heading: G.4 Measuring transformer bias toward tabular policies
sections.text: This section studies how a transformer’s expressibility and implicit bias relate to those of myopic policies. To this end, we conduct two experiments: first, we generate random tabular policies with different ( n b , n f ) (n_{b},n_{f}) windows and use them as a teacher for dense/supervised transformer training. The transformer architecture is the one used throughout the paper: one transformer block layer, four heads, model width 256 256 , rotary position encoding, 791,296 791{,}296 parameters, vocabulary 8 8 . We trained three seeds for each of the eight classes of Table 3 , 24 24 runs in all, and used no regulator: the objective is cross-entropy against the teacher’s own emission at every emitted position, with Adam at learning rate 3 × 10 − 4 3\times 10^{-4} and batch 1024 1024 . In Table 3 we report two numbers per class, both measured on held-out inputs with the transformer generating from its own emissions. The first, agreement , is the fraction of emitted tokens that match the teacher’s at the end of training; the second is the number of gradient steps needed to bring that agreement to 0.999 0.999 , that is to 0.1 % 0.1\,\% error. sections.heading: G.6 Correlations and tying induce local reward maxima
sections.text: Here we discuss two separate mechanisms which trap spin and RLVR models. As a reminder, we say a policy is trapped if no single-cell change raises the reward and no path of reward-neutral single-cell changes reaches a policy from which one does. One way of inducing such traps comes from the shortcut learning perspective: when a simpler heuristic is available for solving the task, the model may commit to a heuristic strategy from which any change towards a better generalizing solution is locally harmful. To induce this option for our task, we introduce input correlation by drawing inputs from a Markov chain having a k k -chance of emitting the same token and a random chance for all other tokens. Notably, correlations also invalidate elements of our proof in App. E . Similarly, introducing tied policies invalidates our proof, and so we consider those as well. This appendix establishes numerically that both these augmentations have a finite chance of introducing traps. With correlated inputs, the models are small enough to settle the question by complete enumeration: at T ≤ 8 T\leq 8 the policy space has at most 2 30 = 1.1 × 10 9 2^{30}=1.1\times 10^{9} members, so every policy is visited, and every local maximum can be classified. The entire set of traps is therefore known rather than sampled. Traps are rare — above 99.99 % 99.99\,\% of local maxima have a cost-free exit. Notwithstanding, the Monte-Carlo chain reaches a trapped state in about one run out of eight, evidence that traps carry large basins. Every trap turns out to be one of a small family of shortcut policies that discard one or two input positions. That family is generated by the correlation, and both of its reward spectra are geometric in 2 ​ k − 1 2k-1 : a policy that discards m m input positions scores 1 2 ​ ( 1 + ( 2 ​ k − 1 ) m ) \tfrac{1}{2}(1+(2k-1)^{m}) , which at k = 0.9 k=0.9 gives 0.90 0.90 and 0.82 0.82 for m = 1 , 2 m=1,2 , and the escape barriers take the values 0.04 × ( 2 ​ k − 1 ) j 0.04\times(2k-1)^{j} . Next we consider tied tabular policies with uncorrelated inputs. For the ( 0 , 3 ) (0,3) tied class at T = 7 T=7 , full enumeration of codes is too costly. Instead, we ran many Monte Carlo chains till saturation (see below). For each chain endpoint we performed a search over its zero-loss neighbourhood. The certification procedure is the following. Call the shelf of a policy the connected component containing it of the graph whose nodes are policies and whose edges are single-cell changes with exactly zero reward difference, and call a shelf node an exit if it admits a single-cell change that strictly raises the reward. Starting from the endpoint we search its shelf breadth-first, evaluating at every node all single-cell changes (of which there are 4,525 × 4 4{,}525\times 4 ), which both tests for an exit and generates the next set of neutral edges. We comment that all reward differences are exact re-simulations rather than the first-order field, which is exact for untied tables but not under tying. The search is capped at 10 5 10^{5} shelf nodes. A policy whose shelf is exhausted with no exit found is certified : no chain of non-losing single-cell changes ever improves it. One that reaches the cap first is reported as bounded , a weaker statement. Following this procedure, we ran Monte-Carlo on twelve different initializations at temperature τ = 10 − 6 \tau=10^{-6} for 20 ​ k 20k sweeps. None of the twelve reaches the optimum. They freeze at twelve distinct rewards between 0.830 0.830 and 0.976 0.976 , mean 0.897 ± 0.044 0.897\pm 0.044 . In every one of the twelve the reward is unchanged from 5 × 10 3 5\times 10^{3} sweeps to 2 × 10 4 2\times 10^{4} — identical to machine precision, not merely non-improving. Ten of the twelve are certified as above, and two reach the maximal node count and are reported as bounded. The shelves are small and simply structured — between 1 1 and 768 768 nodes, of diameter at most 9 9 , with sizes that factor as products of small integers, so neutral moves do not unlock further ones — and two of the certified endpoints have a shelf of a single node, meaning no single-cell change of any kind, improving or flat, exists at rewards of 0.976 0.976 and 0.938 0.938 . Affiliation: Racah Institute of Physics Affiliation: The Hebrew University of Jerusalem Email: noa.rubin@mail.huji.ac.il Zohar Ringel Affiliation: Racah Institute of Physics Affiliation: The Hebrew University of Jerusalem Email: zohar.ringel@mail.huji.ac.il Abstract Despite the importance of reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR), the extent to which it can learn new reasoning capabilities remains debated. Here we study the optimization landscape of RLVR on algorithmic tasks, such as iterated group and quasigroup multiplication. To this end, we map entropy-regularized RLVR over myopic tabular policies onto an energy-based (spin-glass) model over deterministic policies. This mapping upper-bounds what RLVR can achieve, and lets us rigorously characterize the landscape in this tabular setting. We show, both theoretically and experimentally, that for a wide class of models and tasks with uncorrelated inputs, this landscape is benign, containing no local minima that could trap RLVR training. Rather, the practical difficulty of these tasks appears to stem, at least in part, from issues such as diffusive barriers and gradient-estimation error in traversing the landscape. These are genuine obstacles that can prevent a solution from being found, but they are distinct from the landscape itself being rugged. We show that these obstacles can often be mitigated through the choice of entropy regulator. Consistent with this theory, we find that a transformer trained from scratch, using only last-token rewards, successfully learns an algorithmic chain of thought for iterated non-Abelian group multiplications. 1 Introduction Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR), policy-gradient training against an automatically checkable success signal, is the main tool behind recent improvements in the reasoning of large language models ( DeepSeek-AI, 2025 ; Yu and others, 2025 ) . Whether it produces genuinely new reasoning, or mainly reweights behavior already present in the pretrained model, is debated ( Yue and others, 2025 ; Wu et al., 2026 ; Wen et al., 2026 ; Tsilivis et al., 2025 ) . Behind this debate sit open optimisation questions about RLVR itself. Due to the credit assignment problem, intermediate tokens receive little to no direct signal, and sampled gradients are noisy ( Yu and others, 2025 ; Tao et al., 2025 ; Han and Yang, 2026 ; Li et al., 2026 ) . Such hurdles can be, in principle, addressed by larger batches, dynamic sampling, and difficulty curricula ( Yu and others, 2025 ; Jiang et al., 2025 ) , but these are not generic cures. Curricula, for instance, are subject to primacy bias and shortcut learning ( Nikishin et al., 2022 ; Liu et al., 2023 ) . Indeed, practitioners routinely describe runs as “trapped in a local optimum” ( Wang and others, 2025b ; Jin et al., 2026 ) . This brings to question the complexity and ruggedness of RLVR landscapes. Such analyses of reinforcement learning exist for specialized settings (see related literature), which show that optimizing policies with bounded memory is NP-hard in the worst case ( Littman, 1994 ; Mundhenk et al., 2000 ; Vlassis et al., 2012 ) . However, worst-case statements say little about typical instances. For random constraint satisfaction problems, analysis of the typical case was pushed forward by applying statistical mechanics approaches based on spin-glass theory. For instance, spin-glass theory traced typical-case algorithmic hardness to the geometry of the solution landscape, which above certain thresholds breaks into many separated clusters and local minima ( Mézard et al., 2002 ; Krzakala et al., 2007 ; Zdeborová and Krzakala, 2016 ) , inspiring rigorous mathematical approaches ( Gamarnik, 2021 ) . Building a similar bridge between spin-glass theory and RLVR is thus a desirable goal. As a toy setting to approach this goal, we focus on a simple class of algorithmic tasks consisting of iterated quasigroup and group multiplication ( Liu et al., 2023 ; Merrill et al., 2024 ; Li et al., 2024 ; Grazzi et al., 2025 ; Marchetti et al., 2026 ) . This choice is partially motivated by a simplistic reading of what pretraining provides: a set of skills ( Michaud et al., 2024 ) the model can execute individually, together with the problem of composing them in the right order. Taking the skills to be the elements of a finite group or quasigroup and composition to be its operation, “learning to reason” becomes evaluating a product of T T elements presented in sequence, with one intermediate token emitted per element and reward only if the final token is the correct product. As model classes, we use myopic tabular policies (myopic in the sense of DeWeese and Qu (2026) ) that read a bounded window of the input together with their own recent tokens. While such myopic bias is obviously a crude approximation to that of a transformer, the workhorse of RLVR applications in reasoning, it has several merits: It fleshes out culprits in the RLVR loss itself rather than in the policy parametrization. It exhibits some of the qualitative features seen in transformer traps for our tasks, while permitting essentially exact numerics. In this work, we provide a novel spin-glass perspective on RLVR, which allows an in-depth analysis of the above task with some conclusions carrying over to transformers. In particular, we establish the following results A mapping between RLVR and spin models (Sec. 3 ). We build a dictionary between RLVR and spin-glass models, yielding three results: every local maximum of the reward is continuously connected, without crossing a loss barrier, to a deterministic policy, referred to as a code or spin-configuration (§ 3.1 ); with an entropy regulator, the RLVR loss is provably lower-bounded by the free energy of a corresponding spin-glass energy-based model (§ 3.2 ); and steady states of local dynamics on the spin-glass model’s trapped configurations approximately coincide with RLVR fixed points (§ 3.3 ). Spin-glass model for parity task is solvable (Sec. 4.2 ). We obtain closed expressions for the free energy of the spin-glass model associated with parity at any temperature and depth ( T T ) and find a first-order phase transition at large T T , between strictly random and correct codes. Reward landscapes can be benign (Sec. 4.1 ). We leverage the spin-glass mapping to prove that for simple untied models the reward has no suboptimal local maxima. We show that a simple Monte Carlo sampler of the spin-glass models solves all untied models and tasks without a curriculum. With weight tying and input correlations, the proof breaks down, and indeed we find local maxima. The RLVR–spin-glass gap and regulator choices (Sec. 5 ). We show that RLVR optimization (via exact local policy updates) fails to optimize untied models, while as aforementioned, Monte-Carlo on spin-glass models succeeds. This gap is due to the former’s inability to diffuse over equal reward code landscapes. We show that this gap can be closed with local policy resets to random deterministic policies or strong regulators. Strongly regulated transformers solve the task (Sec. 5.1 ). We show numerically that transformers can easily express and interpolate between untied tabular policies with narrow windows and hence share some of their benign landscape features. We further show transformer trained from scratch on the same task fail when left weakly or moderately regulated, but often yield perfect learning of the task when strongly regulated and augmented by a curriculum to circumvent signal-to-noise issues. Additional related literature. Landscape analyses of reinforcement learning exist for specialized settings: gradient-domination results for complete parameterisations ( Agarwal et al., 2021 ; Bhandari and Russo, 2019 ) , the linear-quadratic regulator ( Fazel et al., 2018 ) , convergence for softmax tabular policies ( Mei et al., 2020 ) , and a study of what entropy regularisation does to small exact-gradient problems ( Ahmed et al., 2019 ) . Our work is close in spirit but distinct from the maximum-entropy formulation of control, in which an entropy-regularised objective is read as inference over a Boltzmann measure on trajectories ( Ziebart et al., 2008 ; Levine, 2018 ; Haarnoja et al., 2018 ) : there the sites are the time steps of a rollout, whereas our ensemble is over policies and the sites are table cells. On the physics side, a glassy phase was demonstrated for an optimal-control landscape ( Day et al., 2019 ) , spin-glass language has been applied by analogy to supervised loss surfaces ( Choromanska et al., 2015 ) , and reinforcement learning has been used as a solver for spin-glass ground states ( Fan and others, 2023 ) . The trapped configurations we certify have antecedents as partial pooling equilibria in signalling games ( Lewis, 1969 ; Crawford and Sobel, 1982 ; Huttegger et al., 2010 ; Skyrms, 2010 ) , as miscoordination of independent learners in common-payoff games ( Panait and Luke, 2005 ; Matignon et al., 2012 ) , and as myopic optima of restricted policy classes ( DeWeese and Qu, 2026 ) . Entropy collapse in RLVR and entropy-management schemes are active empirical topics ( Cui and others, 2025 ; Wang and others, 2025a ; Yang et al., 2026 ) ; the diagnostics here differ in being derived from measured landscape structure rather than fitted to online statistics. The stalls of plain RLVR and their repair by re-randomisation are the multi-step counterparts of partial pooling and its destabilisation by mutation ( Zhang, 2004 ) and are kept from premature fixation by margins acting as mutation. 2 Setting: Task and Models Let 𝒜 \mathcal{A} be a finite alphabet of size q q carrying a binary operation B : 𝒜 × 𝒜 → 𝒜 B:\mathcal{A}\times\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{A} whose multiplication table is a Latin square, i.e. every row and every column is a permutation of 𝒜 \mathcal{A} . Such a structure is a quasigroup ; a group is the special case in which B B is also associative. The input is a sequence x 1 ​ … ​ x T x_{1}\ldots x_{T} drawn uniformly from 𝒜 T \mathcal{A}^{T} (in some expereimental setups we break this assumption and draw correlated inputs), and the target is the left fold s 1 = x 1 , s t = B ⁡ [ s t − 1 , x t ] , target = s T . s_{1}=x_{1},\qquad s_{t}=B[s_{t-1},x_{t}],\qquad\text{target}=s_{T}. (1) We refer to s t s_{t} as the state of the task at step t t . To solve this task, we consider models that sequentially generate an output sequence y = ( y 1 , … , y T ) y=(y_{1},\ldots,y_{T}) conditioned on the input x x . At each token index t t , the next token y t y_{t} is drawn from a distribution, or policy, π \pi that can depend on x , y < t , t x,y_{<t},t . An optimal policy is one that perfectly outputs the target, y T = s T y_{T}=s_{T} , regardless of intermediate tokens. In this section, we define two model classes for this task: tabular policies trained with RLVR (Section 2.1 ), and an energy-based model for the distribution of deterministic policies (Section 2.2 ). 2.1 RLVR Optimized Tabular Policies In this class of models, the policy at each timestep relies on a localized context variable c t ​ ( x , y < t ) = ( x t − n p ​ … ​ x t + n f , y t − n y ​ … ​ y t − 1 , t ) c_{t}(x,y_{<t})=(x_{t-n_{p}}\ldots x_{t+n_{f}},y_{t-n_{y}}\ldots y_{t-1},t) (2) which encapsulates a sliding window of the input, a bounded window of previously emitted tokens, and the current time step (ie token index) t t . For the boundary cases, we define for every offset k ∈ { − n p , … , n f } k\in\{-n_{p},\dots,n_{f}\} , x t + k = SEP x_{t+k}=\text{SEP} whenever t + k < 1 t+k<1 or t + k > T t+k>T , and for every k ∈ { 1 , … , n y } k\in\{1,\dots,n_{y}\} , y t − k = SEP y_{t-k}=\text{SEP} whenever t − k < 1 t-k<1 . Consider the untied ( 0 , 0 ) (0,0) window (i.e. c t = ( x t , y t − 1 ) c_{t}=(x_{t},y_{t-1}) ) class on a quasigroup fold with inputs drawn uniformly, and local dynamics that change one cell at a time and accept any change that does not lower J J . First, we show that a collision-free code, one in which no two histories in different task states are ever assigned the same output token, reaches J = 1 J=1 in a finite number of steps that do not decrease the reward. Second, we show how to remove collisions iteratively, without ever decreasing the reward. At a colliding step, every cell is first set to the token that is individually optimal for the true state it leads to. Since there are exactly q q possible true states and q q possible tokens at this step, any two states left sharing a token after this adjustment leave exactly one token unused. We show how the code can be set to route through the unused token without decreasing the reward.
